section.title: Graphs and transformations
section.p: A function is an assignment. A graph is a picture of all those assignments at once.
Each point on the graph of y=f(x) has the form (x,f(x)). The horizontal coordinate is the input. The vertical coordinate is the output.
A graph can show things a formula hides: where a function is positive, where it is zero, where it grows large, and where it has symmetry. It also helps us build new functions from old ones.

subsection.title: Shifts and scalings
subsection.p: Start with the simplest curved graph: f(x)=x^2. Its graph is a parabola. Now compare it with
For every input x, the output of g is 3 more than the output of f. So every point of the graph moves up 3 units:
Thus y=x^2+3 is the graph of y=x^2 shifted upward by 3.
Now compare f(x)=x^2 with
This one is more subtle. The graph shifts to the right, not to the left.

Why? The old function f has its lowest point at input 0, because f(0)=0. The new function h has its lowest point when the inside input is 0: x-2=0, so x=2. The point (0,0) on the old graph becomes (2,0) on the new graph.

figure.caption: Adding outside the function shifts vertically. Changing the input inside the function shifts horizontally.

statement.p: For c\gt 0:

li.p: y=f(x)+c shifts the graph of y=f(x) upward by c.
y=f(x)-c shifts it downward by c.
y=f(x-c) shifts it right by c.
y=f(x+c) shifts it left by c.

subsection.p: Horizontal shifts often feel backward at first. The reason is that the expression inside the function asks: What input should the old function receive? If the new input must satisfy x-c=a, then x=a+c. So old input a appears c units to the right.

statement.p: Let f(x)=\sqrt{x}. Then g(x)=\sqrt{x-4} is the graph of f shifted right by 4.
The domain also shifts. The old domain is [0,\infty). The new function requires x-4\ge 0, so x\ge 4. Thus the domain of g is [4,\infty).

subsection.title: Reflections and stretching
subsection.p: A vertical scaling changes the outputs. For example, if f(x)=x^2, then g(x)=2f(x)=2x^2. Every output doubles. A point (a,f(a)) moves to (a,2f(a)). The graph is stretched vertically by a factor of 2.
If g(x)=\frac{1}{2}f(x), then every output is cut in half. The graph is compressed vertically by a factor of 2.
Horizontal scaling changes the inputs. For example, h(x)=f(2x). The output that used to occur at input a now occurs when 2x=a, so x=\frac{a}{2}. The graph is compressed horizontally by a factor of 2.

statement.p: For A\gt 0, the graph of y=Af(x) is a vertical scaling of the graph of y=f(x) by factor A.
For B\gt 0, the graph of y=f(Bx) is a horizontal scaling by factor \frac{1}{B}.

subsection.p: Again, changes inside the function work in the opposite direction from what the eye may expect. The input Bx reaches old values B times as fast, so the graph is squeezed horizontally when B\gt 1.

statement.p: Let f(x)=\sin x. Then g(x)=\sin(2x) runs through one full sine wave twice as fast as \sin x. Its period is \pi instead of 2\pi. The graph is compressed horizontally by a factor of 2.

subsection.p: Reflections are special scalings by -1:

li.p: The graph of y=-f(x) is the reflection of y=f(x) across the x-axis: (a,f(a))\mapsto (a,-f(a)).
The graph of y=f(-x) is the reflection of y=f(x) across the y-axis: (a,f(a))\mapsto (-a,f(a)).

statement.p: Let f(x)=x^2. Compare g(x)=2f(x-3) with r(x)=2f(x)-3.
The first function is g(x)=2(x-3)^2. It shifts the parabola right by 3, then stretches vertically by 2.
The second function is r(x)=2x^2-3. It stretches vertically by 2, then shifts downward by 3.
These are not the same function. For example, g(0)=2(0-3)^2=18, but r(0)=2\cdot 0^2-3=-3.
Small changes in the formula can mean different geometric changes.

subsection.title: Even and odd symmetry
subsection.p: Some graphs have symmetry around the vertical axis. Others have symmetry around the origin.
The function f(x)=x^2 satisfies f(-x)=(-x)^2=x^2=f(x). So the outputs at x and -x are the same. The graph is symmetric across the y-axis.

The function g(x)=x^3 satisfies g(-x)=(-x)^3=-x^3=-g(x). So the output at -x is the negative of the output at x. The graph has origin symmetry: rotating it 180^\circ around the origin gives the same graph.

statement.p: Suppose the domain of f is symmetric about 0: whenever x is in the domain, so is -x.
The function f is even if f(-x)=f(x) for every x in the domain.
The function f is odd if f(-x)=-f(x) for every x in the domain.
The functions x^2, x^4, and \cos x are even.
The functions x, x^3, and \sin x are odd.
The function f(x)=x^2+x is neither even nor odd, because f(-x)=x^2-x, which is not equal to f(x)=x^2+x, and is not equal to -f(x)=-x^2-x.

paragraphs.title: A small consequence
paragraphs.p: If f is odd and 0 is in its domain, then f(0)=0. Indeed,
But -0=0, so f(0)=-f(0). Thus 2f(0)=0, and therefore f(0)=0.
So an odd function whose graph includes x=0 must pass through the origin.

Symmetry is not only pretty. It saves work. If an even function is known for x\ge 0, then it is known for x\le 0. If an odd function is known for x\ge 0, then the other half is determined by sign change.

subsection.title: Reading intercepts, sign, and intervals from a graph
subsection.p: A graph is a picture of outputs. But many questions about a function are really questions about intervals of inputs:
The graph answers these questions visually.

statement.p: The domain is the set of x-values covered by the graph.
The range is the set of y-values reached by the graph.
The x-intercepts are the points where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis. They occur when f(x)=0.
The y-intercept occurs at x=0, if 0 is in the domain.
The function is positive where the graph lies above the x-axis, and negative where it lies below the x-axis.

example.title: Intercepts and sign of a cubic polynomial

statement.p: Consider
The zeros are visible from the factored form: x=-2, x=1, and x=3. These are the x-intercepts.
The y-intercept is p(0)=\frac{1}{5}(2)(-1)(-3)=\frac{6}{5}. So the graph crosses the y-axis at \left(0,\frac{6}{5}\right).

figure.caption: Zeros divide the x-axis into intervals. On each interval, the graph is either above or below the axis until it crosses again.

statement.p: The zeros divide the real line into four intervals: (-\infty,-2), (-2,1), (1,3), and (3,\infty). From the graph, or from the signs of the factors, we find:
Notice the difference between a point and an interval: p(-2)=0 is a statement about one input. But p(x)\gt 0 on (-2,1) is a statement about infinitely many inputs.

subsection.p: Calculus will often turn a question about a whole graph into questions about intervals. Where is the function increasing? Where is it decreasing? Where is it concave up? Where does it have a largest value?
For now, we only need the first graph-reading skills: intercepts, sign, domain, range, and transformations.

subsection.title: A graph can suggest, but not prove
subsection.p: Graphs are honest when drawn carefully, but they are not proofs by themselves.
A graphing window can hide behavior. A curve may cross the axis just outside the window. A tiny wiggle may disappear if the scale is too large. A vertical asymptote may look like a steep line.
For example, the functions f(x)=x^2 and g(x)=x^2+0.001\sin(1000x) can look almost identical in a wide viewing window. But the second function has many small oscillations.
The lesson is not to distrust graphs. The lesson is to use them correctly.

remark.title: Visual intuition and proof
remark.p: Graphs guide the eye. Algebra and definitions check the claim.

subsection.p: Transformations let us build many new functions from one familiar function. Next we will build functions in a more algebraic way: by adding, multiplying, dividing, and composing them. Composition is the most hidden of these operations, and later it will force one of the most important derivative rules in calculus.
